Question:

After a recent deployment, production logs show McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer reading request-scoped thread-locals and logging nulls; 8% of requests now lack per-request transport context, causing tool invocation failures.

The integration previously relied on thread-locals to pass data into request customizers. What is the most likely cause?

✓ Correct Answer:

Thread-locals are not present in async customizers; populate McpTransportContext per request — use transportContextProvider for sync and Reactor context/contextWrite for async.

📝 Explanation:

Reactive/async execution does not guarantee request-specific thread identity, so thread-locals can be null inside McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer.

The correct approach is to surface per-request context explicitly: for synchronous/blocking clients provide a McpTransportContext via the transportContextProvider (populating it from thread-locals at call time),and for async/reactive flows put the McpTransportContext into the Reactor context with contextWrite so the async customizer (or ExchangeFilterFunction) can retrieve it (for example via Mono.deferContextual).

This ensures transport code sees request-scoped data regardless of threading model.

🧠 Memorable Takeaway

When code may run on different threads (async/reactive), never rely on thread-locals for request-scoped transport data — explicitly pass a McpTransportContext (transportContextProvider for sync, Reactor context/contextWrite for async) so the customizer always sees the right per-request data.

📖 Concept Explanation

Modern HTTP client integrations must treat per-request metadata as an explicit, first-class context rather than relying on implicit thread-local state.

In synchronous/blocking call paths it’s common to stash information on a ThreadLocal so downstream transport code running on the same thread can read it later; however, reactive and asynchronous runtimes (Reactor/Netty, CompletableFuture pools, event loops) decouple work from the original request thread and reuse long‑lived threads.

That decoupling means thread-local values may be absent or stale when customizers run, producing intermittent nulls or leaking data between requests.

The correct production pattern is to construct and carry a per-request transport context object at the moment the request is initiated so any customizer—sync or async—can access it reliably regardless of which thread executes the customization.

Practically, this means you should create an McpTransportContext for each outgoing call and surface it to the transport layer: in blocking clients provide a transportContextProvider that builds the context at call time, and in Reactor-based flows put the context into the Reactor Context (for example via contextWrite and read it with deferContextual) so asynchronous customizers can retrieve it.

Treat the transport context like the “baton” in a relay: hand it to the transport code explicitly instead of assuming it will travel with the current thread.

This approach composes cleanly with connection pooling, retries and filters because the per-request data is bound to the logical request lifecycle rather than to an execution thread.

There are several practical gotchas to watch for in production.

Do not assume SLF4J MDC or InheritableThreadLocal will solve cross-thread propagation: MDC is thread-local and typically not propagated by Reactor/Netty without extra instrumentation, and InheritableThreadLocal only copies values at thread creation (ineffective with thread pools and dangerous for leaking sensitive data on reused threads).

Avoid introducing blocking bridges to “restore” thread-local behavior: forcing reactive code onto blocking threads undermines throughput and can exhaust resources.

Also be mindful of security and memory concerns—ensure per-request contexts are created and cleared promptly, avoid retaining references in long-lived pools, and consider standardized context-propagation libraries or instrumentation if you must propagate tracing/diagnostic state across executor boundaries.

Incorrect Options:

✗

Put per-request transport data into SLF4J MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) at request entry and read MDC inside McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer to access context.

SLF4J MDC is a logging diagnostic context implemented as thread-local storage; it is not reliably propagated across reactive/non-blocking threads used by async customizers.

Relying on MDC will still produce nulls in Reactor-based flows.

The correct approach is to surface a McpTransportContext per request (transportContextProvider for sync, Reactor context/contextWrite for async).

✗

Wrap async handlers with a blocking bridge so thread-locals are available at customization time; modify the client to use blocking calls for those endpoints.

Forcing async/reactive code onto blocking threads to preserve thread-locals may make the values visible, but it defeats the reactive model: it can exhaust event-loop/thread-pool resources, increase latency,
and reduce throughput.

It’s a wrong conceptual fix — changing threading behavior to accommodate thread-local access instead of surfacing per-request context properly (transportContextProvider / Reactor context) creates stability and performance problems and may still not guarantee the customizer sees the right context if the client internals run on different threads.

✗

Replace ThreadLocal with InheritableThreadLocal so worker threads inherit request-scoped transport data and McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer can read those values during async execution.

InheritableThreadLocal only copies values to a thread at the moment the child thread is created.
Reactive runtimes and async HTTP clients reuse long‑lived thread pools (threads are created long before requests arrive), so values won’t be inherited per request.

This approach therefore produces the same missing/null behavior in many Reactor/Netty deployments and additionally risks leaking sensitive per-request data between requests when threads are reused.

The correct solution is to surface a McpTransportContext explicitly (transportContextProvider for sync, Reactor context/contextWrite for async).

You are setting up an async MCP client using McpClient.async(transport) in a high-throughput production service; ExchangeFilterFunction or McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer must compute per-request auth tokens and metadata.

Calls like client.listTools() are missing headers because the transport context isn't available. What should you do?

✓ Correct Answer:

Invoke async operation with Reactor context: client.listTools().contextWrite(ctx -> ctx.put(McpTransportContext.KEY, McpTransportContext.create(Map.of("some-key","some value"))).put("reactor-context-key","some reactor value"));
ensure ExchangeFilterFunction and McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer use Mono.deferContextual.

📝 Explanation:

You must insert the McpTransportContext into the Reactor context for each async client operation using contextWrite so request-scoped data is available to filters and customizers; doing client.listTools().contextWrite(...

put(McpTransportContext.KEY, ...)) makes the McpTransportContext retrievable by McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer or an ExchangeFilterFunction via Mono.deferContextual, allowing them to compute per-request headers and metadata rather than producing missing or incorrect request values.

🧠 Memorable Takeaway

When you need per-request data for reactive client filters, attach it with contextWrite at the call site and read it inside filters with Mono.deferContextual — that guarantees per-request visibility across Reactor's async/thread-hopping execution without blocking.

📖 Concept Explanation

Reactor’s Context is a per-subscriber, immutable key/value map that travels with a reactive chain across thread hops and connection reuse; it is the correct mechanism for carrying request-scoped metadata (tokens, auth info, correlation IDs, etc.) in non-blocking Reactor-based clients.

You attach values at the invocation site using contextWrite so they become part of that call’s subscription context, and you read them downstream with Mono.deferContextual (or similar APIs) inside filters or request customizers.

Because the context is propagated by Reactor itself, values remain visible regardless of thread scheduling or connection pooling, unlike ThreadLocal or Netty Channel attributes which are tied to a single thread or TCP connection and can be lost or accidentally shared between requests.

In practice this means you should insert any per-request transport object into the Reactor Context on the Mono/Flux returned by the client operation, not into global/shared objects.

Filters and customizers then compose non-blocking operations that query Mono.deferContextual to obtain the context and, if necessary, asynchronously fetch tokens and mutate outgoing requests before delegating.

Important implementation details: Reactor Context is immutable so contextWrite returns a modified view for downstream subscribers; if you apply contextWrite too late in the operator chain it may not be visible to earlier operators.

Also be careful with retries, repeats and new subscriptions — those can create new subscriber contexts, so you may need to apply contextWrite inside a defer to ensure each attempt receives the right per-request data.

From an operational standpoint avoid putting large binary blobs or long-lived mutable state into the Reactor Context; treat it as lightweight per-request metadata.

Do not use blocking calls inside filters to synchronously fetch tokens — instead compose the token acquisition as a Mono that is chained after deferContextual so the whole flow remains non-blocking and back-pressured.

Finally, consider observability and security: bridge Reactor Context to your tracing and MDC systems intentionally (MDC is thread-local and must be set per-subscriber), redact sensitive values if contexts are logged, and implement caching for token fetches to prevent repeated remote calls while preserving correct per-request scoping.

Incorrect Options:

✗

Set McpTransportContext in a ThreadLocal before calling the async client and have your filters read it at request time: TRANSPORT.set(McpTransportContext.create(Map.of("some-key","some value")));
client.listTools(); TRANSPORT.remove();

This tries to reuse a synchronous ThreadLocal for request-scoped data.

In Reactor-based async flows the execution may run on different threads, so ThreadLocal values typically won't be visible inside ExchangeFilterFunction or McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer; you must use Reactor Context propagation (contextWrite / Mono.deferContextual) instead.

✗

Set the McpTransportContext as a Reactor Netty / connection attribute on the underlying HTTP client and have filters read the Netty Channel attribute at request time.

Example: ((ReactorNettyTransport) transport).httpClient().doOnRequest((req, conn) -> conn.channel().attr(McpTransportContext.KEY).set(McpTransportContext.create(Map.of("some-key","some value"))));client.listTools();

This puts per-request data on the Netty Channel (connection) instead of in the Reactor Context.

Channel attributes are tied to a TCP connection and can be shared or reused across multiple requests (connection pooling), so they can leak between requests or be missing when connections are recycled.

Also ExchangeFilterFunction / McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer operate at the reactive client layer and do not reliably read transport-level channel attributes;
the correct concept is to propagate request-scoped data in the Reactor Context (contextWrite / Mono.deferContextual).

✗

Compute and inject auth tokens synchronously inside an ExchangeFilterFunction (blocking call) and set headers immediately.

Example: ExchangeFilterFunction authFilter = (request, next) -> { // blocking synchronous token fetch (e.g., legacy auth client) String token = LegacyAuthClient.getToken(request.headers().asHttpHeaders().getFirst("x-some-in"));ClientRequest mutated = ClientRequest.from(request).header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token).build(); return next.exchange(mutated); }; WebClient.builder().filter(authFilter).build(); client.listTools();

This uses a blocking, synchronous token fetch inside a reactive filter.

While it may appear to inject headers per-request, blocking inside Reactor/Netty event-loop threads causes thread starvation, latency spikes, and possible deadlocks under high throughput.

More importantly for this question, a synchronous fetch in the filter bypasses Reactor Context propagation (it doesn't retrieve McpTransportContext via Mono.deferContextual), so it won't reliably access per-request data placed in the Reactor Context — headers can still be missing or incorrect.

The correct approach is to retrieve McpTransportContext non-blockingly from the Reactor Context (Mono.deferContextual / contextWrite) and compose any token fetch as a non-blocking Mono.

Question:

You are integrating an MCP client into a microservice platform.

Both sync and async HttpClient transports must apply multiple independent request customizers (one adds tracing headers, another adds auth) reliably in production. What should you do?

✓ Correct Answer:

Compose multiple request customizers by wrapping them in DelegatingMcpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer for sync and DelegatingMcpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer for async;
ensure order and avoid mutating shared builders, return copies.

📝 Explanation:

The SDK supports only a single customizer instance per transport configuration, so you must compose behaviors using the provided delegating classes.

Using DelegatingMcpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer for sync transports and DelegatingMcpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer for async transports explicitly chains multiple customizers into one instance that the transport accepts.

Careful ordering and avoiding in-place mutations of shared builders prevents one customizer from unintentionally overriding or breaking another;
returning new builder instances or copies ensures predictable header/auth composition and avoids subtle production bugs.

🧠 Memorable Takeaway

When a transport accepts only one customizer, wrap multiple customizers with the SDK's DelegatingMcpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer or DelegatingMcpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer, preserve order, and avoid in-place mutations by returning copies so tracing and auth apply reliably per request.

📖 Concept Explanation

Many MCP HTTP transports accept exactly one request customizer instance, so to apply multiple independent behaviors (for example, tracing and authentication) you implement a small delegating chain that the transport can accept as that single instance.

The SDK provides explicit delegating implementations — DelegatingMcpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer and DelegatingMcpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer — which call each subordinate customizer in sequence.

Under the hood the delegating customizer simply invokes each child customizer against the request builder or context before the transport sends the HTTP request, effectively flattening multiple responsibilities into the one object the transport expects while preserving per-request composition of headers and metadata.

Operational correctness depends on how those customizers interact with the request builder: order matters because later customizers can see or overwrite headers and other fields set earlier, and shared mutable state is a frequent source of subtle bugs.

In practice each customizer should behave like a pure transformation — take the incoming builder or request representation and return a new or safely modified version rather than relying on in-place side effects.

That makes composition deterministic, simplifies reasoning about header precedence (trace IDs and sampling flags should typically be added before auth headers, or vice versa depending on your needs), and avoids races where concurrent requests see each other’s metadata.

In production you also have to consider async behaviors and context propagation.

Async transports may build and send requests on different threads or event-loop contexts where ThreadLocal-based solutions do not reliably transfer per-request state, so explicit composition via the delegating customizers is safer than global or thread-scoped tricks.

Other practical considerations include where to assemble the delegating chain (startup vs per-client), how to handle failures inside a child customizer (fail-fast vs best-effort), token refresh and rotation semantics, and observability to verify that each outgoing request contains the expected headers.

Treat the delegating pattern as an architectural primitive: assemble deterministic, idempotent customizers, test header precedence and concurrency, and prefer explicit composition over implicit global defaults to avoid leaks, stale credentials, and hard-to-debug production races.

Incorrect Options:

✗

Register multiple OkHttp interceptors (one for tracing, one for auth) on HttpClient used by both sync and async transports; rely on interceptor chain.

This is wrong because MCP transports expect a single request customizer instance and the SDK provides DelegatingMcp*RequestCustomizer classes to compose multiple customizers.

OkHttp interceptors are a different mechanism and won't be wired into the MCP transport configuration, so your tracing/auth interceptors may never run or be applied inconsistently for MCP sync/async clients.

✗

Store tracing/auth metadata in a ThreadLocal/global context and implement a single request customizer that reads those values at send-time instead of composing multiple customizers.

This is wrong because it relies on implicit global/thread-local state rather than explicit composition.

MCP async transports may execute request building on different threads or event loops (and many async frameworks don't preserve ThreadLocal), so metadata can be lost, mixed between requests,or leaked across users.

It's a conceptual mistake: use explicit delegating customizers to compose behaviors deterministically rather than hidden global state which causes concurrency and security bugs in production.

✗

Configure default/global headers on the shared HttpClient (set HttpClient/OkHttp default request headers) to add tracing and auth headers for every outgoing request
instead of composing request customizers.

This can look attractive because it’s simple to set shared headers once on the HttpClient, and it works fine for truly static headers.
But it fails for the real requirements here: tracing headers are per-request (unique trace IDs, sampling flags) and auth tokens often rotate or are user-scoped.

Default/global headers tend to be static or updated globally, which leads to stale or leaked credentials and incorrect trace data.

Some async transports construct requests in ways that don’t pick up or update client-level defaults reliably, and updating defaults concurrently can introduce races.

Finally, this approach sidesteps the MCP SDK’s single-customizer model — relying on client defaults does not provide the deterministic, per-request composition that DelegatingMcp*RequestCustomizer gives you, so you’ll get inconsistent behavior across sync and async MCP transports.
